tagline.text: Cavite's highest peak, where the sea unfolds beyond a parrot's-beak rock

location.label: Location
location.text: Ternate and Maragondon, Cavite Province (bordering Nasugbu, Batangas)

children.text: At about

above sea level, this is Cavite's highest mountain. Climb the forest trail to the summit and a massive rock peak jutting up like a parrot's beak, the western sea, and Manila Bay all come into view at once, making it a top pick for a day hike near Manila.
Mount Pico de Loro rises about

above sea level at the border of Ternate and Maragondon in Cavite Province and Nasugbu in Batangas Province, making it Cavite's highest peak. Its name, Spanish for "parrot's beak," comes from the massive rock outcrop (a monolith) jutting out beside the summit like a beak. Formed by ancient volcanic activity, this rock is such a distinct landmark that it can be seen from ships passing far off in Manila Bay, and it has long served as a marker for sailors.

The mountain lies within the Mts. Palay-Palay–Mataas-na-Gulod Protected Landscape, managed by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). It's one of the few remaining lowland forests in southwestern Luzon, home to Philippine endemic birds, monkeys, and a variety of butterflies. What makes this mountain special is that most of the trail runs beneath dense forest shade before suddenly opening up near the summit to reveal the South China Sea (West Philippine Sea), the Nasugbu coast, and the waters toward Corregidor Island.

At one time, hundreds of people flocked here every weekend, causing serious litter and damage, so the mountain went through several closures and rehabilitations. It now operates under an online advance-booking system, a daily visitor cap, and mandatory guides. Climbing to the top of the monolith by rope, as people once did, is now banned for safety reasons, so the hike has shifted to admiring the rock peak from the summit and viewpoints instead.

It suits beginner-to-intermediate hikers with some experience, expat hiking clubs looking for a proper mountain they can do as a day trip from Manila, and travelers who love mountain scenery with sea views. Even those with limited stamina can manage it by climbing slowly, but with the midday heat and steep sections, it's not a casual stroll.

blocks.title: View the parrot's-beak rock from the summit

children.text: Standing at the summit, the massive rock peak rises right beside you with the sea spreading out behind it. It's the mountain's signature view, and on a clear day the coastlines of Batangas and Cavite appear to stretch on together.

From the jump-off point to the summit, you walk mostly under tree shade. You'll cross streams and pass through bamboo groves and rocky sections, enjoying the forest's changing character along the way.

blocks.title: Early-morning sea of clouds and sunlight

children.text: Set off before dawn in the dry season and you'll find a thin mist settled in the valley below, with the rock at the summit lit by soft morning light.
Being a protected area, there's a good chance of encountering Philippine endemic birds and monkeys. Walk quietly and listen for the sounds of the forest.
From the summit viewpoint you can frame the rock peak and the sea in a single shot. A wide-angle lens or your phone's wide mode comes in handy.
Come down from the mountain and cool off at a beach in Nasugbu or Ternate, about
30–40 minutes
away by car, for the perfect day.
On the way back, stop by Maragondon town, home to an 18th-century church and the house where revolutionary leader Andres Bonifacio was tried.

is the wet season, when the trail turns to slippery mud and leeches can appear in the forest. When a typhoon or heavy rain warning is in effect, the protected area's management suspends all hiking. The protected area is also temporarily closed at times for scheduled rest-and-restoration periods or during high wildfire risk, so always check for notices before you set off.
Weekend and public holiday bookings often fill up 2–3 weeks in advance. If you have a specific date in mind, apply as soon as the booking window opens.

Most people do this as a day hike, but if an early-morning departure isn't appealing, you can stay the night before at a resort on the Ternate or Nasugbu coast. Resorts on the Ternate coast and beach lodgings toward Nasugbu run about
a night, about
20–40 minutes
from the jump-off by car. For an upscale resort, consider the resort cluster on the Nasugbu coast.

There's no shop on the mountain, so bring trail snacks and a packed lunch. After the descent, enjoy grilled fish, shrimp, and sinigang at a Filipino seafood restaurant on the Ternate or Nasugbu coast, or try pancit pusit (squid-ink noodles), a specialty of Cavite City. If you head back via Tagaytay, bulalo and buko pie at the highland restaurant row are also good choices.
You must book an official online reservation before hiking. Without a confirmation and ID on hand, you may be denied entry on site.
There are set operating days, a daily visitor cap, and a cutoff time for entering the trail. Check the protected area management office's official notice again the day before you set off.
Bring at least 2–3 liters of water per person. Unlike in the past, when there used to be a place selling water partway up, you can't count on resupply now.
Wear trekking shoes or running shoes with good grip. The trail mixes rocky sections and dirt paths, so sandals or everyday shoes are dangerous.
Gloves are handy for gripping ropes and rocks. Trekking poles greatly reduce the strain on your knees during the descent.
There's no shade near the summit, so a hat, sunscreen, and long-sleeve arm sleeves come in handy.
Mobile signal is unstable on the mountain, so don't get separated from your group, and save your guide's contact number.
The rule is to carry all your trash back out. Bring a small trash bag in your backpack.
Climbing the parrot's-beak rock (the monolith) is prohibited. Fatal falls have occurred in this section in the past, so never cross the warning line.
Don't stray from the designated trail. Camping, lighting fires, and collecting plants or animals within the protected area are violations that can be penalized.
The risk of heatstroke is high at midday. If you feel dizzy or get a headache, rest in the shade immediately and replenish fluids and electrolytes.
During the wet season, the muddy slopes are very slippery and leeches appear. Bring long socks and anti-leech spray.
If you push your schedule and descend late in the afternoon, the forest darkens quickly. Bring a headlamp and stick to the turnaround time your guide sets.
Illegally hiking in via a bypass route without a reservation is subject to enforcement, and rescue is difficult if an accident occurs.
